hero.title: Two years of Project 2025: what got done, what it cost, and who paid
hero.dek: The Heritage Foundation’s 900-page plan was disowned by the candidate and executed by the president. By every tracker’s count more than half of it is in place. The Supreme Court has struck down its boldest pieces, its authors run the agencies they wrote about, a quarter of the senior staff has turned over, and the people it reached run from 65,000 immigrants in detention to a school in Minab, Iran.

sections.title: The verdict, in short
sections.text:
Project 2025 worked, in the sense its authors meant. The independent trackers that score the Mandate for Leadership line by line put it between 53 and 55 percent implemented by this autumn [1][2], and the Heritage Foundation itself told donors in June that “over half” of it was in place [3]. The administration carried out the plan’s core: a civil service that can be fired at will, agencies hollowed by layoffs and shuttered by executive order, a deportation machine funded at a scale no Congress had contemplated, and an executive that treats appropriations, independent commissions and the press corps as things to be managed rather than obeyed [8][9].

It did not work in the sense the voters were promised. Prices were not down on day one; the war in Ukraine did not end in 24 hours; the “worst first” deportations swept up a population three-quarters of whom had no criminal conviction [38][39]. And where the plan met the Constitution it mostly lost: the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs 6–3 [15], held the birthright-citizenship order unconstitutional 5–4 [18], and refused to let the president fire a Federal Reserve governor [17], even as it handed him the power to fire everyone else [16].

The cost is where this page spends most of its time, because it is where the numbers are least often put together. Deaths in immigration detention in 2025 matched the worst year ICE has ever recorded, and the fiscal year that ended in September surpassed it [35][36][37]. A study in The Lancet projected 14 million additional deaths by 2030 from the dismantling of USAID [47]. The Congressional Budget Office put the health law’s coverage loss at nearly 11 million people [49]. And on the first day of the war with Iran that the campaign had promised would never come, an American missile destroyed an elementary school in Minab; Airwars identified 123 children among the dead [43][44]. The people responsible are named on these pages, with what they did and what became of them.

sections.title: What Project 2025 is
sections.text:
Mandate for Leadership: The Conservative Promise is a 30-chapter policy book published by the Heritage Foundation in April 2023, edited by Paul Dans and Steven Groves, with a foreword by Heritage’s president, Kevin Roberts [13][14]. Each chapter takes an agency or a cluster of them, is written by a former official or an ally who expected to return, and ends in a list of instructions for the first days of a new administration. Its five sections run from “Taking the reins of government” (the White House, the budget office and the personnel agencies) through defense, the “general welfare” departments and the economy to the independent regulators [13].

The copy a reader is most likely to have seen in Congress’s files is the one entered into the record of a House Oversight subcommittee hearing on Sept. 25, 2024 [12], at which Paul Winfree, the author of the Mandate’s Federal Reserve chapter, was a Republican witness; Rep. Melanie Stansbury put the book into the record and called it “the playbook that was put forward by the conservative community for the next administration” [10][11]. The full text is mirrored by Democracy Docket and the Internet Archive [13].

The candidate ran away from it. “I know nothing about Project 2025,” Donald Trump wrote on July 5, 2024. “I have no idea who is behind it” [6]. In his debate with Kamala Harris that September he said he had not read it and would not [7]. Within a week of the inauguration, Time counted nearly two-thirds of the new executive actions mirroring the Mandate, and CNN counted 36 of 53 [4][5]. On Oct. 2, 2025, during the shutdown, the president announced a meeting with “Russ Vought, he of PROJECT 2025 Fame” [7]. Dans, by then out of Heritage, told NPR in January 2026: “Every day that President Trump rolls out another Project 2025 item, it’s really an endorsement of our work” [8].

sections.title: How much of it is done
sections.text:
Three groups keep line-by-line counts. The volunteer tracker at project2025.observer scores 321 objectives across 34 agencies; on Nov. 8, 2026 it listed 141 completed, 70 in progress and 110 not started, a weighted 55 percent, with the most recent completion dated Aug. 12 [1]. The Center for Progressive Reform and Governing for Impact, scoring 532 recommended executive actions at 20 domestic agencies, found 283 initiated or completed at the one-year mark, 53 percent [2]. Heritage’s own fundraising email in June claimed 53 percent [3]. The pace is the other finding: the observer’s log shows completions falling from about 13 a month in the first half of 2025 to about one a month through 2026, as the easy executive orders ran out and the courts and the calendar caught up [1].

The Watch’s own scorecard, below and on its own page, is narrower and stricter. It tracks the proposals from each chapter that changed the most lives or the most law, and it scores them against what stands today, not what was announced: a thing the courts have enjoined is “blocked,” not done; a thing done in a weaker form is “partial.” Chapter 3 (the civil service) and Chapter 9 (USAID) are the plan’s clearest successes; Chapter 24 (the Federal Reserve) and the birthright-citizenship order are its clearest defeats; the tariffs, which the Mandate presented as a debate between two authors rather than a plan, were imposed, struck down and partly re-imposed under other statutes [15].

sections.title: Where the courts stepped in
sections.text:
More than 550 lawsuits have been filed against the administration’s actions [50], and the pattern of the big ones is consistent: the Supreme Court gave the president his personnel powers and took away his policy shortcuts. On June 29, 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, the court overruled Humphrey’s Executor and let the president remove the heads of independent agencies at will [16]; the same day, 5–4, it held in Trump v. Cook that he could not remove Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook [17]. A day later, in Trump v. Barbara, Chief Justice Roberts wrote for a 5–4 court that the order ending birthright citizenship was unconstitutional [18]. In February the court had already held, 6–3, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs, and the Court of International Trade ordered refunds with interest [15].

Lower courts did the rest of the work. Judges found the dismantling of Voice of America unlawful [25], enjoined the Guard deployments to Portland and Chicago, where the Supreme Court declined to intervene [21], and the Ninth Circuit upheld the order ending the federalization of California’s Guard [22]. The prosecutions of James Comey and Letitia James collapsed when the prosecutor who brought them was found to have been unlawfully appointed; the appeals were argued in September [19]. Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s charges were dismissed as a vindictive prosecution [20]. A judge found the Justice Department had likely violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act [26]. On Nov. 2, 2026, the day before the midterms, the Supreme Court refused the department’s bid to set aside some 20,000 California ballots [27].

The administration won where the Mandate had planned for it to win. The court let the reductions in force proceed [23], let the Education Department’s wind-down continue, and allowed the pocket rescission of $4 billion in foreign aid that the Impoundment Control Act was written to prevent [24]. The contempt inquiry into the March 2025 deportation flights, which the government has told the D.C. Circuit were ordered by Kristi Noem, was argued en banc on Sept. 29 and is pending [20].

sections.title: What was promised, and what happened
sections.text:
PolitiFact’s MAGA-Meter, which tracks 75 second-term promises, rated 15 kept, 21 stalled, 31 in the works and 5 broken as of Oct. 26, 2026 [52]; the White House’s own count that week was 127 promises kept. The Watch’s list is shorter and sorted by consequence: the spoken commitments that moved votes, in the words they were spoken, against the record.

The pattern is a government that kept the promises it could keep by itself and broke the ones that depended on the world. The Jan. 6 pardons, the border emergency, Schedule F and the return to the office were done in days. The 24-hour peace in Ukraine, “prices down on day one,” gasoline under $2, energy bills cut in half, “we’re not cutting Medicaid” and “criminals first” are broken, by the administration’s own numbers where they exist [52][53]. The promise to avoid new wars ended with a raid on Caracas in January and a war with Iran in February [45][46]. The one price that fell was eggs.

sections.title: Who did it
sections.text:
The Mandate’s authors came back for the agencies they wrote about. Russell Vought, who wrote the chapter on the Executive Office of the President, runs the Office of Management and Budget and the impoundments, the shutdown layoffs and the rescissions that chapter called for [7][8]. Brendan Carr wrote the FCC chapter and chairs the FCC. Paul Atkins contributed to the financial-regulators chapter and chairs the SEC; John Ratcliffe is credited on the intelligence chapter his former chief of staff wrote and runs the CIA; Tom Homan, a credited contributor, is the border czar; Karoline Leavitt trained on Project 2025’s videos for the job she held until August [8][9]. Stephen Miller, whose America First Legal sat on the project’s advisory board until he asked for its name to be removed, becomes White House chief of staff on Nov. 9 [33].

Each official’s card below lists the actions that map to the Mandate, with the reporting behind them, and the controversies that followed. The scorecard, the court cases and the promises on this site link back to the officials responsible for each.

sections.title: Who is gone
sections.text:
The first year was quieter than the first term; the second has not been. Brookings’ Kathryn Dunn Tenpas counted 29 percent turnover among the senior White House staff in 2025, against 35 percent in 2017 and about 10 percent for the six presidents before Trump, and no cabinet departures at all [29]. By Sept. 30, 2026 her tracker stood at 56 percent, with three of the 15 cabinet secretaries gone [28]; the Partnership for Public Service counted 27 Senate-confirmed departures from the cabinet departments in 18 months, against 11 in the first term [30].

The cabinet broke in the spring. Kristi Noem was removed from Homeland Security on March 5, two days after a bipartisan grilling over the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal agents in Minneapolis [31]. Pam Bondi was out as attorney general on April 2 [32]. Lori Chavez-DeRemer resigned from Labor amid an inspector general’s inquiry; Tulsi Gabbard left as director of national intelligence in June; John Phelan was fired as Navy secretary and Gen. Randy George as Army chief of staff in April. Joe Kent resigned as director of the National Counterterrorism Center in protest of the Iran war, saying Iran “posed no imminent threat” [34]. After Republicans lost both chambers on Nov. 3, Susie Wiles resigned as chief of staff [33]. The Watch’s list below is every senior departure it could source, with the stated reason and the successor; it is updated each week.

sections.title: What it did to people
sections.text:
The Mandate’s immigration chapter asked for detention at a scale that would require new camps, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act paid for them: $45 billion for detention alone, enough for 116,000 to 125,000 beds, a 308 percent increase over the 2024 budget by the American Immigration Council’s reckoning [40]. The detained population passed 70,000 in January 2026, the most since records begin; 74 percent of them had no criminal conviction [38]. Deaths in custody in calendar 2025 numbered 31 to 33 depending on who counts, against 11 in 2024, matching the record set in 2004 [35][36]; fiscal 2026 ended with 36 or 37, the most in ICE’s history [37]. ProPublica documented 506 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents; the Marshall Project counted more than 6,200 children [41][42]. Two citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot dead by federal agents in Minneapolis in January 2026; no one has been charged [31].

Abroad, the dismantling of USAID in the plan’s first months was followed by a projection in The Lancet of more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030, 4.5 million of them children under five [47]; a Boston University counter of deaths already attributable to the cuts passed 750,000 in January 2026 and was retired a month later at 781,343 [48]. Secretary Rubio told Congress in May 2025 that “no children are dying” [11]. The war with Iran that began Feb. 28, 2026 has killed, by Iran’s health ministry, 3,468 people including 376 children, and 23 American troops [45][46]. The school in Minab is its own dossier below, with the claim this page was asked to check: 123 is the number of children Airwars identified among at least 157 dead [43][44].

At home, the CBO scored the health law at 10.9 million more uninsured by 2034 and more than $1.2 trillion in Medicaid and food-stamp cuts [49]; the 43-day shutdown that followed furloughed 900,000 workers and cut off November food stamps for 41 million people until the courts intervened [50]; the enhanced insurance subsidies expired on Jan. 1, 2026 after a 51–48 Senate vote [49]. The effective tariff rate reached about 27 percent in April 2025, the highest in a century, before the courts cut it to 12 percent [51]. About 200,000 federal workers were gone by August 2025 and 9 percent of the workforce by March 2026 [51].

sections.title: Who made money
sections.text:
The stock market did what it usually does, with a detour. The S&P 500 fell 7.9 percent in the first hundred days, the worst start since Nixon, lost $6.6 trillion in the two days after the April 2 tariffs, and gained 9.5 percent on April 9 after the president posted “THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY” four hours before pausing them [57][58]. It ended 2025 up 16 percent, the weakest first presidential year in two decades [58], set a record of 7,818.93 on Oct. 6, 2026 as the 10-year Treasury yield passed 5 percent, and lost 4.4 percent on Nov. 5, the day after the midterms, its largest one-day dollar loss ever [55][56]. On Nov. 6 it closed at 7,376.86, 23 percent above the last close before the inauguration [54]. The Federal Reserve, under its new chair Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time in three years, with inflation at 3.4 percent [66].

The GEO Group, which runs more of ICE’s beds than any other company, is the plan’s purest trade. Its shares closed at $14.18 the day before the 2024 election and $36.46 the day after the inauguration [59][60]. It then spent a year under its post-election high while the contracts came in — Delaney Hall in Newark at $1 billion, North Lake in Michigan, Adelanto, Big Horn in Colorado — and fell below its pre-election price on Feb. 12, 2026 after the Minneapolis killings and a weak quarter [60]. It recovered to $29.28 by June on the “largest amount of new business we have won in a single year in our company’s history,” in its chairman’s words, with ICE at 48 percent of revenue [61][62]. CoreCivic’s chief executive told investors that “never in our 42-year company history” had demand looked like this [59].

The president’s family took in roughly $2 billion in 2025 by the New York Times’ accounting, most of it from the $TRUMP memecoin and World Liberty Financial, and his 2025 disclosure, released in June, showed $635 million in memecoin royalties alone [65]. Tesla’s shareholders approved a $1 trillion pay package for Elon Musk in November 2025, then watched the stock fall to a 2026 low of $298.32 in July and lose 10.8 percent on Nov. 5 [63][64].

sections.title: The richest man and the election
sections.text: Elon Musk’s money in the 2024 election, his four months running the Department of Government Efficiency, the Wisconsin Supreme Court race, the June 2025 break with the president and the vote-count theories that circulated afterward are the subject of a separate page, built as a documentary with the filings, the dates and the videos. In this first sprint it holds what could be verified: Tesla’s share price and corporate record and the DOGE figures. The Federal Election Commission totals, the Wisconsin numbers, the conspiracy claims and what election officials and fact-checkers found about them are queued for the next sprint, when the research budget resets; nothing on that page will be stated without a filing or a report behind it.

Broadcast and documentary footage from official channels is queued for the next sprint, when it can be verified and embedded with its source.

sections.title: The record, by month
sections.text: Everything dated on these pages — the executive actions, the rulings, the promises as they were made, the departures, the deaths and the market’s turns — is merged into one stream on the timeline page, filterable by kind. The last two weeks of it:

method:
The Watch built this section on Nov. 8, 2026 from seven research passes, each confined to what it could read and link: the Mandate’s text and the trackers that score it; the administration’s actions against each chapter; the court dockets and the trackers kept by Just Security, Lawfare and SCOTUSblog; the cabinet roster and every departure Brookings, the Partnership for Public Service and the press recorded; the campaign’s spoken commitments against PolitiFact, AP and Bloomberg; the human cost from ICE’s own death notices, TRAC, KFF, HRANA, Airwars, the Lancet and the CBO; and the markets from AP’s daily index reports and the companies’ filings. Where a figure rests on a secondary page (several Wikipedia hubs, a mirror of an AP column) the receipts say so, and the weekly sprint replaces it with the primary source when it can be read.

Statuses are judged against what stands today. “Done” means carried out and in force; “blocked by courts” means an injunction or a ruling is in force against it; “partial” means done in a weaker form or in part; “reversed” means done and undone. For the promises: “kept,” “partly kept,” “broken,” “stalled,” “reversed” and “too early.” For the courts: who prevailed at the latest ruling. The research budget for the first sprint ran out before several items could be sourced — Musk’s election spending, the documentaries, the private-prison donations, the 2026 measles and jobs figures among them — and those are listed as gaps rather than filled from memory. The record is kept as JSON in the repository’s news/mandate/data folder, checked by build.py, and refreshed in weekly sprints through December.

tour.caption: Taking the reins of government
tour.sub: The White House, the budget office and the personnel agencies: Schedule F, the layoffs, the impoundments. The plan’s clearest wins.

tour.caption: Chapter 3: the civil service
tour.sub: Tens of thousands of career posts reclassified as at-will; about 200,000 workers gone by August 2025. The Supreme Court let the reductions in force proceed.

tour.caption: The common defense
tour.sub: Homeland Security, State, the intelligence agencies, the media agencies and USAID. The deportation machine, the dismantling of Voice of America and of foreign aid.

tour.caption: Chapter 9: USAID
tour.sub: Dismantled in the plan’s first months. The Lancet projected 14 million additional deaths by 2030; a Boston University counter passed 750,000 before it was retired.

tour.caption: The general welfare
tour.sub: Education, Health, Justice, Energy, the EPA and the rest. The Education Department wound down; Medicaid cut; the prosecutions of adversaries that the courts threw out.

tour.caption: The economy
tour.sub: Treasury, Commerce, Trade and the Federal Reserve. The tariffs were imposed and struck down; the Fed’s independence survived by one vote.

tour.caption: Independent regulatory agencies
tour.sub: The FCC, the FTC, the SEC and the CFPB. Humphrey’s Executor is overruled; the president may now fire the commissioners at will.
